title: The reaction quotient and equilibrium calculations
summary: The [[reaction-quotient|reaction quotient]], $Q$, is the equilibrium expression filled in with the concentrations a mixture has right now. Comparing $Q$ with $K$ tells you which way the mixture will react. The [[equilibrium-law|equilibrium law]] also lets you work out an equilibrium mixture from its starting amounts, and $\Delta G^\ominus = -RT\ln K$ links the position of equilibrium to [[gibbs-energy|Gibbs energy]].

goals.text: Calculate the [[reaction-quotient|reaction quotient]] $Q$ for a mixture and compare it with $K$ to predict which way the mixture reacts.
Use an ICE table and the [[equilibrium-law|equilibrium law]] to find $K$, or an unknown equilibrium concentration, from initial amounts.
Explain and use the approximation $[\text{reactant}]_{\text{initial}} \approx [\text{reactant}]_{\text{eqm}}$ when $K$ is very small.
Convert between $\Delta G^\ominus$ and $K$ with $\Delta G^\ominus = -RT\ln K$, and use the sign of $\Delta G$ to explain which way a mixture reacts.

before.prompt: A $\pu{3.00 dm3}$ flask holds $\pu{0.450 mol}$ of hydrogen. What is the concentration of hydrogen in $\pu{mol dm-3}$?
before.hint: Divide the amount in [[mole|moles]] by the volume in $\pu{dm3}$.

before.prompt: For $\ce{CO(g) + Cl2(g) <=> COCl2(g)}$ at equilibrium, $[\ce{CO}] = \pu{0.0200 mol dm-3}$, $[\ce{Cl2}] = \pu{0.0300 mol dm-3}$ and $[\ce{COCl2}] = \pu{0.150 mol dm-3}$. Calculate $K$.
At constant temperature and pressure, a reaction has a negative $\Delta G$. What does this tell you?
before.hint: The sign of $\Delta G$ decides whether a change happens on its own.
before.explain: Negative $\Delta G$ means spontaneous. It says nothing about rate, and $\Delta G = 0$ at equilibrium. Revise it in {{lesson:4.7}}.

blocks.text: $K$ only describes a mixture at [[dynamic-equilibrium|dynamic equilibrium]]. But most mixtures you make in a flask are not at equilibrium yet. You need a way to tell which way such a mixture will go.
The trick is to fill in the [[equilibrium-constant|equilibrium constant]] expression with the concentrations the mixture has at that moment. The number you get is called $Q$.

blocks.statement: The value of the equilibrium expression worked out from the concentrations present in a mixture at one moment, whether or not that mixture has reached equilibrium.
blocks.plain: The same fraction as $K$, but for the mixture as it is right now.

blocks.tex: \ce{aA + bB <=> cC + dD} \qquad Q = \frac{[\ce{C}]^{c}\,[\ce{D}]^{d}}{[\ce{A}]^{a}\,[\ce{B}]^{b}} \text{ (concentrations at that moment)}

blocks.text: $K$ is fixed at a given temperature. $Q$ changes as the mixture reacts. A mixture always reacts so that $Q$ moves towards $K$, and it stops changing when $Q = K$.

blocks.statement: If $Q < K$, there is a net forward reaction until $Q = K$. If $Q > K$, there is a net backward reaction until $Q = K$. If $Q = K$, the mixture is already at equilibrium.
blocks.why: Products are on top of $Q$. If $Q$ is too small, the mixture has too little product, so more forms; if $Q$ is too large, it has too much, so some turns back into reactants.

blocks.alt: A horizontal arrow labelled value of Q, running from more reactants on the left to more products on the right. A vertical line in the middle is labelled Q equals K, at equilibrium, no net change. On the left, labelled Q less than K, an arrow points right towards the line: net forward reaction, products form, Q rises. On the right, labelled Q greater than K, an arrow points left towards the line: net backward reaction, reactants form, Q falls.
blocks.caption: Whichever side it starts on, a mixture reacts so that $Q$ moves towards $K$.

blocks.question: For $\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$, $K = 46.0$ at $\pu{764 K}$. A mixture at $\pu{764 K}$ contains $[\ce{H2}] = \pu{0.0250 mol dm-3}$, $[\ce{I2}] = \pu{0.0100 mol dm-3}$ and $[\ce{HI}] = \pu{0.150 mol dm-3}$. Calculate $Q$ and determine the direction in which the mixture reacts.
steps: Write the expression from the equation: $Q = \frac{[\ce{HI}]^{2}}{[\ce{H2}][\ce{I2}]}$.
Substitute the concentrations at this moment: $Q = \frac{0.150^{2}}{0.0250 \times 0.0100} = \frac{0.0225}{0.000250}$.
Compare: $90.0 > 46.0$, so $Q > K$. The mixture has too much $\ce{HI}$ for equilibrium, so there is a net backward reaction: $\ce{HI}$ decomposes until $Q$ falls to $46.0$.

blocks.text: $Q$ also explains what [[le-chateliers-principle|Le Châtelier's principle]] predicts ({{lesson:5.9}}). Adding or removing a substance changes $Q$ but not $K$, so the mixture reacts until $Q$ equals $K$ again.

blocks.question: The hydrogen iodide mixture above is left until it reaches equilibrium at $\pu{764 K}$. Then more hydrogen is injected, at constant volume and temperature. Explain, in terms of $Q$ and $K$, how the mixture responds.
steps: "Explain" needs the reason, so say what happens to $Q$ first, then what follows.
$[\ce{H2}]$ is on the bottom of $Q = \frac{[\ce{HI}]^{2}}{[\ce{H2}][\ce{I2}]}$, so raising it makes $Q$ smaller.
The temperature has not changed, so $K$ is still $46.0$.
blocks.answer: Hydrogen is in the denominator of the expression, so adding it makes Q smaller than K. The temperature is unchanged, so K stays the same. Because Q is less than K, there is a net forward reaction and more hydrogen iodide forms. As it forms, Q increases until it equals K again, and a new equilibrium is reached.

verify.truth: Adding H2 lowers Q below K (K fixed at fixed T), so net forward reaction until Q = K again.

blocks.text: Getting the comparison back to front. $Q < K$ means too little product, so the forward reaction wins. Check by asking whether the top of $Q$ needs to grow or shrink.

blocks.prompt: For a reaction at $\pu{600 K}$, $K = 2.4 \times 10^{-2}$. A mixture at $\pu{600 K}$ has $Q = 5.0 \times 10^{-3}$. What happens?

options.text: There is a net forward reaction until Q equals K.
There is a net backward reaction until Q equals K.
Nothing happens: the mixture is at equilibrium.
K falls until it equals Q.

blocks.explain: $5.0 \times 10^{-3} < 2.4 \times 10^{-2}$, so $Q < K$: products form until $Q$ rises to $K$. $K$ itself is fixed at $\pu{600 K}$.

verify.truth: There is a net forward reaction until Q equals K.

blocks.prompt: For $\ce{2NOBr(g) <=> 2NO(g) + Br2(g)}$, a mixture contains $[\ce{NOBr}] = \pu{0.0400 mol dm-3}$, $[\ce{NO}] = \pu{0.0100 mol dm-3}$ and $[\ce{Br2}] = \pu{0.0200 mol dm-3}$. Calculate $Q$ to 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: Products on top. Two of the species have a coefficient of 2.

blocks.text: The [[equilibrium-law|equilibrium law]] links the equilibrium concentrations through $K$. So if you know enough of them, you can find the rest, or $K$ itself.
The tool is an ICE table: one row each for Initial amounts, the Change, and Equilibrium amounts, with one column per species.
1. Write the balanced equation and fill in the initial amounts. A product not added at the start has $0$.

2. Fill in the changes. They must be in the mole ratio of the equation: if $x$ of a reactant with coefficient 1 is used up, $2x$ of one with coefficient 2 is used up. Reactants go down; products go up.
3. Add each change to the initial amount to get the equilibrium amount.
4. Divide each equilibrium [[mole|amount in moles]] by the volume to get its [[molar-concentration|molar concentration]], then substitute into the expression for $K$.
Putting amounts in moles straight into $K$. Unless the volume is $\pu{1 dm3}$, divide each amount by the volume first.

blocks.question: $\pu{0.600 mol}$ of $\ce{CO}$ and $\pu{1.40 mol}$ of $\ce{H2}$ are sealed in a $\pu{2.50 dm3}$ vessel and heated: $\ce{CO(g) + 2H2(g) <=> CH3OH(g)}$. At equilibrium the vessel contains $\pu{0.180 mol}$ of $\ce{CH3OH}$. Calculate $K$ at this temperature.
steps: Change (mol): $\ce{CH3OH}$ rises by $0.180$, so $\ce{CO}$ falls by $0.180$ and $\ce{H2}$ by $2 \times 0.180 = 0.360$.
$K = \frac{[\ce{CH3OH}]}{[\ce{CO}][\ce{H2}]^{2}} = \frac{0.0720}{0.168 \times 0.416^{2}} = 2.4765\ldots$ Give 3 significant figures.

blocks.text: Sometimes you know $K$ and the starting mixture, and need the equilibrium mixture. Then the change is an unknown, $x$. Exam questions avoid quadratic equations, so they are set up to give a simple equation.

blocks.question: Hydrogen and iodine, each at $\pu{0.200 mol dm-3}$, are heated to $\pu{764 K}$ in a sealed flask: $\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$, $K = 46.0$. Calculate $[\ce{HI}]$ at equilibrium.
steps: Let $x$ be the fall in $[\ce{H2}]$. Then $[\ce{H2}] = [\ce{I2}] = 0.200 - x$ and $[\ce{HI}] = 2x$ at equilibrium.
$K = \frac{(2x)^{2}}{(0.200 - x)^{2}} = 46.0$. Both sides are perfect squares, so take the square root: $\frac{2x}{0.200 - x} = \sqrt{46.0} = 6.7823\ldots$

blocks.prompt: In $\ce{N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g)}$, $[\ce{N2}]$ falls by $\pu{0.040 mol dm-3}$ on the way to equilibrium. By how much, in $\pu{mol dm-3}$, does $[\ce{NH3}]$ rise?
blocks.hint: Use the mole ratio of $\ce{N2}$ to $\ce{NH3}$.
blocks.explain: $1$ mol of $\ce{N2}$ gives $2$ mol of $\ce{NH3}$, so $[\ce{NH3}]$ rises by $2 \times 0.040 = 0.080$. $0.12$ is the fall in $[\ce{H2}]$.

blocks.prompt: For $\ce{CO(g) + 2H2(g) <=> CH3OH(g)}$, $K = 14.5$ at a lower temperature. At equilibrium, $[\ce{CO}] = \pu{0.0500 mol dm-3}$ and $[\ce{H2}] = \pu{0.120 mol dm-3}$. Calculate $[\ce{CH3OH}]$ in $\pu{mol dm-3}$ to 3 significant figures.

blocks.text: If $K \ll 1$, the position of equilibrium lies far to the left. Starting from reactants only, a tiny fraction of each reactant reacts.

So $x$, the amount that reacts, is negligible next to the initial concentration. For a reactant that starts at $\pu{0.0100 mol dm-3}$, you can write $0.0100 - x \approx 0.0100$, which turns a hard equation into an easy one.

blocks.statement: When $K$ is very small and the mixture starts as reactants only, $[\text{reactant}]_{\text{eqm}} \approx [\text{reactant}]_{\text{initial}}$.
blocks.why: So little reactant is used up that subtracting it makes no difference at the precision of the data.

blocks.text: Only make this approximation for reactants. You still solve for the products, which start from zero and are what you are looking for.

blocks.question: Air in a hot engine contains $[\ce{N2}] = \pu{0.0520 mol dm-3}$ and $[\ce{O2}] = \pu{0.0140 mol dm-3}$ before any reaction. For $\ce{N2(g) + O2(g) <=> 2NO(g)}$, $K = 6.40 \times 10^{-5}$ at $\pu{1700 K}$. Calculate $[\ce{NO}]$ at equilibrium at $\pu{1700 K}$.
steps: $K$ is very small, so take $[\ce{N2}] \approx 0.0520$ and $[\ce{O2}] \approx 0.0140$.
Check: $x = \frac{[\ce{NO}]}{2} \approx 1.08 \times 10^{-4}$, under 1% of $0.0140$, so the approximation was fair.

blocks.question: Explain why the approximation $[\ce{O2}]_{\text{eqm}} \approx [\ce{O2}]_{\text{initial}}$ was justified in the last example, and why it could not be used for the hydrogen iodide mixture, where $K = 46.0$.
steps: Link the size of $K$ to how much reactant is used up.
Use the numbers: $x$ was about $1.08 \times 10^{-4}$ against $0.0140$.
For hydrogen iodide, $x$ was about $0.154$ against $0.200$.
blocks.answer: K is very small, so the position of equilibrium lies far to the left. Only a tiny amount of oxygen reacts, less than 1% of the initial concentration. Subtracting it changes the concentration by a negligible amount, so the equilibrium concentration is approximately equal to the initial concentration. For hydrogen iodide, K is greater than 1, so most of the reactants react and the change is far too large to ignore.

verify.truth: K very small: equilibrium far left, tiny x, so [O2] barely changes. HI has K > 1, so x is large.

blocks.prompt: Each reaction below starts with only reactants. For which value of $K$ is $[\text{reactant}]_{\text{eqm}} \approx [\text{reactant}]_{\text{initial}}$ a fair approximation?
blocks.hint: The approximation needs almost no reactant to be used up.
blocks.explain: Only a very small $K$ means hardly any reactant reacts. With $K$ near or above 1, a large share of the reactants is used up.

blocks.prompt: $[\ce{HBr}]$ starts at $\pu{0.0600 mol dm-3}$, with no products. For $\ce{2HBr(g) <=> H2(g) + Br2(g)}$, $K = 2.50 \times 10^{-11}$. Calculate $[\ce{H2}]$ at equilibrium, in $\pu{mol dm-3}$, to 3 significant figures.
blocks.explain: $K = \frac{x^{2}}{0.0600^{2}}$, so $x = 0.0600 \times \sqrt{2.50 \times 10^{-11}} = 3.00 \times 10^{-7}$. That is tiny next to $0.0600$, so the approximation holds.

blocks.text: In {{lesson:4.7}} you met the standard [[gibbs-energy|Gibbs energy]] change, $\Delta G^\ominus$. Like $K$, it measures the position of equilibrium, and one can be calculated from the other.

This is in section 1 of the data booklet, so you don't need to memorise it. $R$ is the [[gas-constant|gas constant]], $\pu{8.31 J K-1 mol-1}$ (section 2), so $\Delta G^\ominus$ comes out in $\pu{J mol-1}$. $T$ is in kelvin, and $\ln$ is the natural log.
To find $K$ from $\Delta G^\ominus$, rearrange: $K = \mathrm{e}^{-\Delta G^\ominus/RT}$, with $\Delta G^\ominus$ in joules.

blocks.statement: $\Delta G^\ominus < 0$ gives $K > 1$: products are favoured. $\Delta G^\ominus > 0$ gives $K < 1$: reactants are favoured. $\Delta G^\ominus = 0$ gives $K = 1$.
blocks.why: $\ln K$ is positive when $K > 1$ and negative when $K < 1$, and the minus sign in $-RT\ln K$ flips it.

blocks.question: Use section 13 of the data booklet to calculate $K$ at $\pu{298 K}$ for $\ce{CO(g) + H2O(g) <=> CO2(g) + H2(g)}$.
steps: $\Delta G^\ominus = \sum \Delta G_{\text{f}}^\ominus(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta G_{\text{f}}^\ominus(\text{reactants})$. $\Delta G_{\text{f}}^\ominus$ of an element such as $\ce{H2}$ is $0$.
$\ln K = \frac{-\Delta G^\ominus}{RT} = \frac{28000}{8.31 \times 298} = 11.307\ldots$
$K = \mathrm{e}^{11.307} = 8.14 \ldots \times 10^{4}$. $\Delta G^\ominus$ is only known to 2 significant figures, so give $K$ to 2.

$K \gg 1$, so products are strongly favoured at $\pu{298 K}$. The reaction is still slow at this temperature: industry heats it and adds a [[catalyst|catalyst]], which speeds it up but does not change $K$.

blocks.text: The booklet's other equation, $\Delta G = \Delta G^\ominus + RT\ln Q$, gives $\Delta G$ for a mixture that is not at equilibrium. It connects $Q$ and $K$ to the direction of reaction.
Substitute $\Delta G^\ominus = -RT\ln K$ and combine the logs: $\Delta G = RT\ln Q - RT\ln K = RT\ln\frac{Q}{K}$. So the sign of $\Delta G$ depends only on whether $Q$ is below or above $K$.

blocks.question: Use the two Gibbs energy equations in the data booklet to explain why a mixture with $Q > K$ undergoes a net backward reaction.
steps: Combine the equations: $\Delta G = RT\ln\frac{Q}{K}$.
Decide the sign of $\ln\frac{Q}{K}$ when $Q > K$, then link the sign of $\Delta G$ to spontaneity.
blocks.answer: Substituting the second equation into the first gives the Gibbs energy change as RT ln(Q/K). If Q is greater than K, then Q/K is greater than 1, so ln(Q/K) is positive. RT is positive, so the Gibbs energy change is positive. The forward reaction is not spontaneous, but the backward reaction is, so there is a net backward reaction. This continues until Q equals K, when the Gibbs energy change is zero.

verify.truth: Delta G = RT ln(Q/K); Q > K makes ln(Q/K) > 0, so Delta G > 0 and the backward reaction is spontaneous until Q = K.

blocks.text: Mixing units or logs. $R$ is in joules, so convert $\Delta G^\ominus$ from kJ to J, and use $\ln$, not $\log_{10}$.

blocks.prompt: For a reaction at $\pu{650 K}$, $K = 3.60 \times 10^{-3}$. Calculate $\Delta G^\ominus$ in $\pu{kJ mol-1}$, with its sign, to 3 significant figures.
blocks.explain: $\Delta G^\ominus = -8.31 \times 650 \times \ln(3.60 \times 10^{-3}) = \pu{+30392 J mol-1} \approx \pu{+30.4 kJ mol-1}$. Positive, as it must be for $K < 1$.

blocks.prompt: A reaction has a positive $\Delta G^\ominus$ at $\pu{400 K}$. Which statement about its equilibrium at $\pu{400 K}$ is correct?

options.text: K is less than 1, so reactants are favoured.
K is greater than 1, so products are favoured.
K is zero, so no products form.

blocks.explain: Positive $\Delta G^\ominus$ needs $\ln K < 0$, so $0 < K < 1$. $K$ is never negative or zero: some products always form.

verify.truth: K is less than 1, so reactants are favoured.

blocks.text: $Q$ is the equilibrium expression with the concentrations at that moment. $Q < K$: net forward. $Q > K$: net backward. $Q = K$: at equilibrium.
ICE table: initial amounts, changes in the mole ratio of the equation, equilibrium amounts. Divide by the volume before substituting into $K$.
When $K$ is very small and the mixture starts as reactants only, $[\text{reactant}]_{\text{eqm}} \approx [\text{reactant}]_{\text{initial}}$.
$\Delta G^\ominus < 0$: $K > 1$. $\Delta G^\ominus > 0$: $K < 1$. For any mixture, $\Delta G = RT\ln\frac{Q}{K}$, so $\Delta G < 0$ exactly when $Q < K$.

mistakes: Reading the comparison back to front. $Q < K$ means too little product, so the net reaction is forward.
Substituting amounts in moles into $K$ when the volume is not $\pu{1 dm3}$. Convert every amount to a concentration first.
Writing changes that ignore the equation. If $x$ of $\ce{CO}$ reacts in $\ce{CO + 2H2 <=> CH3OH}$, then $2x$ of $\ce{H2}$ reacts.
Using $[\text{reactant}]_{\text{eqm}} \approx [\text{reactant}]_{\text{initial}}$ when $K$ is not very small.
Leaving $\Delta G^\ominus$ in kJ next to $R$ in J, or using $\log_{10}$ instead of $\ln$.
Saying that adding a reactant changes $K$. It changes $Q$; only temperature changes $K$.
examTips: "Determine the direction" a mixture reacts: calculate $Q$, compare it with $K$ in words or symbols ($Q < K$), then state the net direction. The comparison earns the mark, not the conclusion alone.
"Calculate $K$" from starting amounts: show the equilibrium amounts, the concentrations and the substituted expression. A wrong earlier value used correctly can still earn later marks.
With $\Delta G^\ominus = -RT\ln K$, write the substitution with $\Delta G^\ominus$ in J, and give $\Delta G^\ominus$ with its sign and units.
If a question would seem to need a quadratic, look again: either $K$ is very small, so the approximation applies, or both sides are perfect squares.
